{{short description|American mathematician}}
'''Charles Earl Rickart''' (1913 &ndash; 17 April 2002) was an American mathematician,<ref name=YaleObit>{{cite news|newspaper=Yale Bulletin & Calendar|date=10 May 2002|volume=30|issue=29|title=Long-time teacher Charles Rickart dies; helped introduce 'new math'|url=http://www.yale.edu/opa/arc-ybc/v30.n29/story17.html|url-status=bot: unknown|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20090402054412/http://www.yale.edu/opa/arc-ybc/v30.n29/story17.html|archivedate=2 April 2009}}</ref> known for [[Rickart space]]s.
 
Rickart was born in [[Osage City, Kansas]], and earned his B.A. and M.A. from the [[University of Kansas]]. In 1941, he received his PhD from the [[University of Michigan]] under [[Theophil Henry Hildebrandt]] with the thesis ''Integration in a Convex Linear Topological Space''.<ref name=RickartGen>{{MathGenealogy|id=5191|title=Charles Rickart}}</ref> Rickart was for two years the Benjamin Pierce Instructor at [[Harvard University]]. He joined the [[Yale University|Yale]] mathematics faculty in 1943, served as chair of the department from 1959 to 1965, became the first Percey F. Smith Professor of Mathematics in 1963, and retired in 1983.<ref name="YaleObit"/>

Rickart did research on [[Banach algebra]]s and was the author of three books. In the late 1950s and early 1960s, he was one of the pioneers in introducing the "[[new math]]" into American schools.<ref name="YaleObit"/> His doctoral students include [[Samuel Merrill III]].<ref name="RickartGen"/>

He died in [[North Branford, Connecticut]] where he lived, survived by his wife, Annabel Erickson Rickart, three sons, and four grandchildren.<ref name="YaleObit"/>
